ety.text: From Middle English aspect, from Latin aspectus (“look, sight; appearance”), from aspiciō (“see; catch sight of; inspect”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + speciō (“look, look at, behold; observe”).

senses.d: Any specific feature, part, or element of something.
ex: Japan's aging population is an important aspect of its economy.

senses.d: The way something appears when viewed from a certain direction or perspective.
ex: The stone has a greenish aspect in this light.
Given the limitations of planar representation[…] The painter is constantly forced to choose one aspect over the other.

senses.d: The way something appears when considered from a certain point of view.
ex: in certain aspects [ = in certain respects]

senses.d: A phase or a partial, but significant view or description of something.

ex: In Knots they ſtand, or in a Rank they Walk, / Serious in Aſpect, earneſt in their Talk: […]
It is Stephen Gardiner, black and scowling, his aspect in no way improved by his trip to Rome.

senses.d: Position or situation with regard to seeing; that position which enables one to look in a particular direction; position in relation to the points of the compass.
ex: The house has a southern aspect, i.e. a position which faces the south.
This town affords a good aspect toward the hill from whence we descended ; nor does it deceive us ; for it is handsomely built […]

senses.d: A grammatical quality of a verb which determines the relationship of the speaker to the internal temporal flow of the event which the verb describes, or whether the speaker views the event from outside as a whole, or from within as it is unfolding.
The relative position of heavenly bodies as they appear to an observer on earth; the angular relationship between points in a horoscope.
The personified manifestation of a deity that represents one or more of its characteristics or functions.
To have a particular aspect or type of aspect.

From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).

senses.d: To have a strong desire or ambition to achieve something.
ex: to aspire to / for / after / to do something; to aspire that something happens
He aspires to become a successful doctor.

senses.d: To go as high as, to reach the top of (something).
ex: Thus ſhall my heart be ſtil combinde with thine, / Untill our bodies turne to Elements: / And both our ſoules aſpire celeſtiall thrones.
Mercutio’s dead! / That gallant spirit hath aspired the clouds,

senses.d: To move upward; to be very tall.
ex: In midſt of which a ſumptuous Temple ſtands, / That threats the ſtarres with her aſpiring toppe.
Seas that restlessly aspire, / Surging, unto skies of fire;

From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”). Displaced native Old English eorþtyrewa (literally, "earth-tar").

senses.d: A sticky, black to brown and highly viscous liquid or semi-solid, composed almost entirely of bitumen with small mineral particles, that is present in most crude petroleums and in some natural deposits.
ex: The mining of asphalt was big business in this area in the early twentieth century.
